docs.title: ADR-0001: Architecture Pattern Selection for Online Ticket Flash Sale System
Context
docs.text:
The Online Ticket Flash Sale System is a public-facing event ticketing platform used by ticket buyers, venue administrators, system operators, and event organizers. The system must support event browsing, real-time ticket inventory queries, flash-sale order placement, payment integration, order lifecycle management, automated unpaid stock releases, system monitoring, and audit logging.

The system has several architecturally significant requirements: - It must handle extreme traffic spikes (high QPS/TPS) during ticket sale ignition and deadlines; - It must remain highly available during active ticket sale periods; - It must enforce absolute zero over-selling (No Over-selling) to maintain data consistency under massive concurrency; - It must protect sensitive user authentication, payment, and transaction data; - It must keep all purchase attempts, order states, and administrative actions auditable; - It must integrate reliably with third-party payment gateways; - It must provide rapid, low-latency responses (under 50 ms for request ingestion) without locking persistent storage; - It must support dynamic flash-sale events with varying seat rules, quota limits, and pricing structures.

A single architectural style must therefore balance extreme scalability, low latency, maintainability, reliability, security, auditability, and implementation complexity.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
We will use Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) as the Primary Architectural Paradigm, combined with CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) for Read/Write Path Separation.

The system will be divided into clear components based on business capabilities. User-facing query workflows will use synchronous API and caching communication when an immediate response is required. Background order processing and stock mutations will use asynchronous event-driven communication.

Main system components include: - Client Web/Mobile Application; - API Gateway & Dynamic Token Validation Service; - User Identity & Rate Limiting Service; - Ticket Inquiry & Read-Side Cache Service (CQRS Read Path); - Redis Lua Pre-deduction Engine (CQRS Write Path - Producer); - Kafka Event Broker / Message Queue; - Asynchronous Order Processing Worker Cluster (EDA Consumer); - Relational Database (Primary-Secondary MySQL with Read/Write Splitting); - Delay Queue / Unpaid Order Timeout Service; - Notification Service (WebSocket Push); - Audit Logging & Monitoring Service; - Third-Party Payment Gateway Integration.

Synchronous communication will be used for actions such as user authentication, event browsing, real-time ticket availability checks (Redis cache hits), and payment gateway status synchronization.

Asynchronous communication will be used for actions such as queueing purchase commands, Order Persistence, unpaid stock release timers, WebSocket status notifications, audit logging, and metric tracking.

docs.title: Y-Statement
docs.text: In the context of building an Online Ticket Flash Sale System as a high-concurrency event ticketing platform, facing extreme traffic spikes, strict zero over-selling constraints, auditability requirements, third-party payment integration, and low-latency user feedback targets, we decided on an Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) combined with CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation), and rejected a simple monolithic architecture, a traditional layered architecture, a full microservices architecture, and a pure event-driven architecture, to achieve extreme scalability, ultra-low latency, high availability, zero over-selling safety, auditability, and reliable background peak shaving, accepting higher system complexity than a monolith and the need to manage eventual consistency and asynchronous workflows, because the system needs clear separation of read/write responsibilities and scalable queueing workflows without the full operational burden and network latency overhead of complete microservices.

docs.title: Option 1: Monolithic Architecture
docs.text: A monolithic architecture would place all ticket inquiry, order placement, payment processing, and audit functions into a single deployable application database unit.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Simple initial development and local testing.
  • Single database transaction guarantees simple immediate consistency.
  • Lower operational complexity and deployment overhead for small-scale applications.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Cannot scale ticket purchase functions independently during high-concurrency flash sale peaks.
  • High database lock contention under simultaneous write requests leads to thread pool exhaustion and system failure.
  • Third-party payment delays or database bottlenecks directly degrade the entire application.
  • High risk of inventory over-selling under unhandled race conditions.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: A monolith is entirely unsuitable for flash-sale scenarios because synchronous database writes cannot handle extreme burst traffic spikes.

docs.title: Option 2: Traditional Layered Architecture
docs.text: A layered architecture strictly organizes code vertically into Presentation Layer, Business Logic Layer, and Data Access Layer with synchronous calls.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Well-known standard structure with clear separation of code concerns.
  • Easy for development teams to organize.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• End-to-end synchronous call chains (Client -> Gateway -> Service -> Database) block threads while waiting for DB IO.
  • Thread starvation occurs immediately when thousands of requests hit the database simultaneously.
  • Does not separate high-volume read traffic from high-concurrency write traffic.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Layered architecture fails under flash-sale workloads because synchronous vertical execution blocks system resources during demand spikes.

docs.title: Option 3: Full Microservices Architecture
docs.text: A full microservices architecture splits each business capability into an independently deployable service, each managing its own isolated database.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Independent scalability and deployment for each business service.
  • Clear domain ownership across large engineering teams.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• High operational complexity requiring Kubernetes, service meshes, and complex CI/CD pipelines.
  • Distributed transactions (e.g., SAGA/TCC) across microservice databases introduce latency and implementation risk.
  • Increased network hop latency is undesirable for sub-50ms flash sale responses.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Full microservices introduce excessive operational burden and distributed transaction complexity without solving the fundamental high-concurrency database peak-shaving problem.

docs.title: Option 4: Pure Event-Driven Architecture
docs.text: A pure event-driven architecture makes every interaction, including ticket browsing and login, asynchronous via event buses.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Maximum decoupling and asynchronous execution.
  • Excellent for background execution, audit logging, and audit history.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Poor user experience for synchronous actions (e.g., browsing tickets or logging in).
  • Higher complexity for user-facing request-response workflows.
  • Difficult to guarantee immediate read consistency where expected.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: Pure event-driven models are unsuitable because ticket queries require immediate synchronous responses via cache.

docs.title: Option 5: Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) + CQRS Pattern
docs.text: This option separates the system into a high-throughput CQRS Read Path (Redis cache) and an EDA Write Path (Redis Lua pre-deduction + Kafka queue + asynchronous workers).

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• CQRS Read Path: 99% of ticket browsing hits Redis/CDN directly, achieving $100,000+\text{ QPS}$ without touching the relational database.
  • EDA Write Path: Flash-sale purchase commands are ingested in memory via Lua scripts and pushed to Kafka in $<50\text{ ms}$, shaving traffic peaks.
  • Zero Over-selling Guarantee: Redis Lua scripts ensure atomic stock deduction; Kafka sequential partition consumption prevents database race conditions.
  • Fault Isolation: Database slowness does not block request ingestion in Kafka.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• Requires managing eventual consistency between queue completion and user UI updates.
  • Higher complexity than a monolith, requiring event handling, retries, and dead-letter queues.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text: This hybrid option provides the optimal architecture for flash sale systems, balancing high throughput, low latency, data safety, and peak shaving.

docs.title: Positive Consequences
docs.text:
• Flash-sale purchase endpoints ingest massive traffic spikes asynchronously without crashing persistent databases.
  • Read operations scale independently using Redis cache clusters.
  • Zero over-selling is guaranteed through atomic memory operations and queued processing.
  • WebSocket pushes notify users asynchronously once workers complete order persistence.
  • Unpaid orders are automatically released back to stock using delay queues after 15 minutes.
  • Audit logging is reliably triggered by events without blocking core purchasing logic.

docs.title: Negative Consequences
docs.text:
• System architecture is more complex than a standard monolithic application.
  • Developers must manage eventual consistency and asynchronous messaging logic.
  • Requires infrastructure monitoring for Kafka queue backlogs and Redis memory usage.

docs.title: Risk Mitigation
docs.text:
• Use Redis Lua scripts for atomic stock validation and deduction.
  • Implement database unique composite indexes (User_ID + Activity_ID) to guarantee consumer idempotency.
  • Implement dead-letter queues (DLQ) and retry mechanisms for failed order events.
  • Deploy WebSocket fallback polling for client queue notification redundancy.

docs.title: Impact on Architecture
docs.text: This decision determines the core container and component decomposition: - Client UI Layer (Web/Mobile); - API Gateway & Rate Limiting Container; - CQRS Read Cache Container (Redis Cluster); - Flash Sale Command Producer Container (Lua Script Execution); - Message Broker Container (Apache Kafka); - Asynchronous Worker Consumer Cluster; - Persistence Database (MySQL Primary-Secondary); - Unpaid Order Delay Queue Container; - Notification Container (WebSocket); - Audit Log Storage.

  • FR-3.2: EDA Kafka Event Publication and Queueing
  • FR-3.5: Idempotent Order Persistence and Zero Over-selling
  • FR-4.3: Asynchronous Unpaid Order Stock Recovery
  • NFR-PER-1: $100,000\text{ QPS}$ Read / $50,000\text{ TPS}$ Write Performance Targets
  • NFR-PER-2: Sub-50ms Response Latency for Purchase Ingestion

docs.title: Related Architectural Characteristics
docs.text:
• Scalability
  • Availability
  • Performance & Low Latency
  • Data Consistency & Safety
  • Auditability
  • Fault Tolerance & Peak Shaving
  • Maintainability

docs.title: Final Decision
docs.text: The selected architectural style is Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) with CQRS Pattern. This architecture is appropriate for the Online Ticket Flash Sale System because it fulfills all key requirements of a high-concurrency ticketing platform: extreme peak shaving, low-latency ingestion, strict zero over-selling, isolated read/write scaling, and reliable background order persistence.

docs.title: 1.1 Purpose
docs.text: This Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document provides a comprehensive and rigorous description of the requirements for the Online Ticket Flash Sale System. Based on the IEEE Standard 830 format, this document outlines the architectural constraints (Event-Driven Architecture and CQRS pattern), functional requirements, and non-functional quality attributes to guide software architects, developers, testers, and academic evaluators.

docs.title: 1.2 Document Conventions
docs.text:
• Standard Markdown formatting is applied throughout the document.
  • Functional requirements are uniquely identified using the format FR-<Category>.<ID>.
  • Non-functional requirements are identified using the format NFR-<Category>.<ID>.
  • Architectural markers such as [EDA] denote asynchronous event-driven paths, and [CQRS] denote Command Query Responsibility Segregation paths.

docs.title: 1.3 Intended Audience and Reading Suggestions
docs.text:
• Software Architects: Focus on Section 2 (Overall Description) and Section 5 (Nonfunctional Requirements) to validate the EDA + CQRS architectural pattern selection.
  • Developers: Refer to Section 3 (External Interfaces) and Section 4 (System Features) for module design and coding implementation.
  • QA and Test Engineers: Utilize Section 4 and Section 5 for high-concurrency performance test cases and verification metrics.
  • Academic Evaluators: Review Section 1 for project scope and Section 4 for core domain logic.

docs.title: 1.4 Product Scope
docs.text:
The Online Ticket Flash Sale System is designed to handle extreme burst traffic (e.g., hot concerts, major sports events). Its primary objective is to guarantee system availability, absolute zero over-selling, and low-latency response under massive concurrency.

  • In-Scope:
  • User authentication and dynamic token generation.
  • High-throughput ticket inventory queries via CQRS read-side caching.
  • Asynchronous flash sale order placement and traffic peak-shaving via EDA messaging.
  • Order lifecycle management, payment integration, and automatic stock release for unpaid orders.
  • Out-of-Scope:
  • Physical hardware ticket printer integration.
  • Implementation of third-party banking payment gateways (standard API integration only).

docs.title: 1.5 References
docs.text:
1. IEEE Std 830-1998, IEEE Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications.
  2. Architecture Decision Records (ADR) Standard Repository format: https://github.com/architecture-decision-record/architecture-decision-record
  3. Martin Fowler, Event-Driven Architecture, https://martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html
  4. Martin Fowler, CQRS Pattern, https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CQRS.html

docs.title: 2.1 Product Perspective
docs.text:
The system is a greenfield distributed application built to replace traditional monolithic synchronous architectures that fail under flash-sale traffic spikes. It adopts an Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) as its primary paradigm, coupled with Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS):

  • Read Path: User ticket browsing and inventory checks are served directly by edge CDN and Redis cache clusters, bypassing the primary database to ensure extreme throughput and low latency.
  • Write Path: Ticket purchase commands are published as TicketPurchaseEvent messages into a high-throughput message queue (Apache Kafka), where asynchronous worker threads process orders and persist data safely.

docs.title: 2.2 Product Functions
docs.text:
1. User Authentication & Dynamic Token Distribution: Expose temporary secure URLs and tokens prior to the flash sale to mitigate bot attacks.
  2. Real-time Inventory Inquiry [CQRS Read]: Sharded and pre-warmed cache reads for concurrent availability checks.
  3. Atomic Flash Sale Deduction [CQRS Write / EDA Producer]: Concurrency-safe stock pre-deduction using Redis Lua scripts.
  4. Asynchronous Peak Shaving [EDA Event Queue]: Instantly push purchase events to message queues and return queue status to clients.
  5. Asynchronous Order Persistence [EDA Consumer]: Background workers consume events, validate consistency, and persist orders.
  6. Automatic Timeout Release: Delay queues automatically return un-paid stock back to inventory after 15 minutes.

docs.title: 2.3 User Characteristics
docs.text:
1. General End-Users: Representing over 99% of traffic, accessing the system simultaneously at flash-sale launch with strict expectations for low response latency.
  2. System Administrators: Responsible for event configuration, inventory pre-heating, and monitoring system parameters.
  3. DevOps Engineers: Monitor message queue backlog, cache hit rates, and database CPU loads.

docs.title: 2.4 Operating Environment
docs.text:
• Operating System: Linux (Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS / RHEL 9)
  • Containerization & Orchestration: Docker, Kubernetes (k8s)
  • Caching Layer: Redis 7.x Cluster (Primary-Replica & Sharded)
  • Messaging Middleware: Apache Kafka 3.x
  • Persistence Database: MySQL 8.0 (Primary-Secondary replication with read/write splitting)
  • Network Environment: HTTP/2, WebSocket, CDN edge nodes

docs.title: 2.5 Design and Implementation Constraints
docs.text:
1. Architectural Constraint: Must strictly adhere to the EDA + CQRS decoupling pattern, prohibiting synchronous blocking calls on write paths.
  2. Data Consistency Constraint: Write paths follow eventual consistency while maintaining absolute zero over-selling.
  3. Security Constraint: Must incorporate rate limiting, CAPTCHA, and dynamic URL tokens to defend against script scalpers.

docs.title: 2.6 User Documentation
docs.text:
1. System Integration and API Specification Manual
  2. Flash Sale Event Configuration and Pre-heating Guide
  3. High-Concurrency Emergency Incident Response and Queue Backlog Troubleshooting Handbook

docs.title: 2.7 Assumptions and Dependencies
docs.text:
1. Assumes client network stability and that CDN nodes successfully intercept over 80% of static asset traffic.
  2. Relies on the reliability and high availability of third-party payment gateway webhooks.

docs.title: 3.1 User Interfaces
docs.text:
1. Pre-sale Waiting Interface: Features a countdown timer with the purchase button disabled until sale ignition.
  2. Queue Processing Interface: Displays animated WebSocket/polling status updates reading "Queueing in progress".
  3. Order Payment Interface: Displays an order payment countdown (15 minutes) and payment QR code.

docs.title: 3.2 Hardware Interfaces
docs.text: The system is a pure software distributed architecture with no dedicated hardware interface requirements, running on standard x86_64 or ARM64 cloud infrastructure.

docs.title: 3.3 Software Interfaces
docs.text:
1. Redis API: Executing Lua scripts for atomic in-memory stock management and cache queries.
  2. Kafka Produce/Consume API: Publishing and subscribing to TicketPurchaseEvent streams.
  3. Third-Party Payment API: RESTful over HTTPS for payment status transactions.

docs.title: 3.4 Communications Interfaces
docs.text:
1. Client-Server Communication: Mandatory HTTPS with TLS 1.3 encryption.
  2. Real-time Notifications: WebSocket full-duplex persistent connections for queue results.
  3. Internal Inter-service Communication: gRPC/TCP protocols for high-performance serialization.

docs.title: 4.1 System Feature 1
docs.text:
System Feature 1: User Authentication and Flash Sale Eligibility Verification Priority: High Description: Ensure request legitimacy and intercept malicious scripts or unauthenticated traffic. Functional Requirements:

  • FR-1.1: The system shall support stateless user authentication and fast login verification via JSON Web Tokens (JWT).
  • FR-1.2: The system shall dynamically generate randomized ticketing URL tokens prior to sale commencement to prevent automated script prediction.
  • FR-1.3: The system shall enforce rate limiting based on User ID and IP addresses to prevent high-frequency request floods from single accounts.
  • FR-1.4: The system shall dynamically trigger CAPTCHA challenges under high traffic spikes to scatter burst requests.

docs.title: 4.2 System Feature 2 (and so on)
docs.text:
System Feature 2: Real-time Ticket Inquiry and Multilevel Caching [CQRS Read Path] Priority: High Description: Handle high QPS read traffic before and after the flash sale via robust cache tiers. Functional Requirements:

  • FR-2.1: The system shall pre-heat all ticket details and inventory counts into Redis cache clusters, ensuring read requests do not hit relational databases.
  • FR-2.2: The system shall deploy Bloom Filters to prevent invalid requests from penetrating to the database (cache penetration defense).
  • FR-2.3: The system shall enable local in-memory secondary caching (e.g., Caffeine) for hot keys to mitigate hot-key breakdown issues.
  • FR-2.4: Upon inventory mutation, the system shall asynchronously invalidate or update caches via Pub/Sub mechanisms to guarantee read model consistency.

System Feature 3: Asynchronous Flash Sale Order Placement and Peak Shaving [EDA Write Path] Priority: High Description: Process click-to-purchase commands via in-memory atomic deduction and queue events for asynchronous peak shaving. Functional Requirements:

  • FR-3.1: Upon receiving a purchase request, the system shall invoke a Redis Lua script to validate and pre-deduct inventory atomically in memory.
  • FR-3.2: If memory deduction succeeds, the system shall instantly construct a TicketPurchaseEvent and publish it to the Kafka message queue.
  • FR-3.3: Upon event publication, the system shall immediately return a "Request Accepted, Queueing" response to the client within 50 ms.
  • FR-3.4: Background worker processes shall subscribe to Kafka topics, consuming purchase events asynchronously and sequentially to execute database order creation and stock deduction.
  • FR-3.5: The system shall guarantee idempotency through database composite unique constraints (e.g., User_ID + Activity_ID), completely preventing duplicate purchases and over-selling.
  • FR-3.6: Upon worker processing completion, the system shall asynchronously push success/failure notifications to clients via WebSocket.

System Feature 4: Order Lifecycle Management and Automatic Stock Release Priority: Medium Description: Automatically cancel unpaid orders and rollback inventory after expiration. Functional Requirements:

  • FR-4.1: Upon successful purchase reservation, the system shall generate a pending payment order and initiate a 15-minute countdown timer.
  • FR-4.2: If payment is completed within 15 minutes, the system shall update order status to "Paid" and trigger electronic ticket generation events.
  • FR-4.3: If payment is overdue past 15 minutes, the system delay queue shall trigger an OrderTimeoutEvent.
  • FR-4.4: Upon receiving timeout events, workers shall cancel orders and restock the pre-deducted inventory back into Redis and MySQL.

docs.title: 5.1 Performance Requirements
docs.text:
• NFR-PER-1 (Throughput): The read path must support peak traffic of no less than $100,000 \text{ QPS}$; the write path must support burst event ingestion of no less than $50,000 \text{ TPS}$.
  • NFR-PER-2 (Latency): The 99th percentile ($P_{99}$) response time for purchase API request ingestion and event queue publishing must be under $50 \text{ ms}$.
  • NFR-PER-3 (Scalability): Message queue consumer workers must support dynamic horizontal scaling (HPA) based on queue backlog metrics.

docs.title: 5.2 Safety Requirements
docs.text:
• NFR-SAF-1 (Zero Over-selling): Under any concurrency level, the total sum of successfully sold orders in the database must never exceed the pre-defined total inventory limit (0% over-selling rate).
  • NFR-SAF-2 (Fault Isolation): Database outages or high latencies must not impede Kafka message queue ingestion of purchase events, isolating write caches from read caches.

docs.title: 5.3 Security Requirements
docs.text:
• NFR-SEC-1 (Data Transmission Security): All external API communications must enforce TLS 1.3 protocol encryption.
  • NFR-SEC-2 (Anti-Scraping Protection): The system must enforce API rate limiting, restricting single users to a maximum of 2 requests per second per endpoint.

docs.title: 5.4 Software Quality Attributes
docs.text:
• NFR-QUA-1 (Availability): Overall system availability during flash sale peaks must be no less than $99.99\%$.
  • NFR-QUA-2 (Consistency): Data synchronization delay between CQRS read and write paths must complete within $3\text{ seconds}$.
  • NFR-QUA-3 (Maintainability): Core components must be fully decoupled via messaging middleware, ensuring storage layer or business logic modifications do not impact event producers.

docs.title: 5.5 Business Rules
docs.text:
• BR-1 (Purchase Quota): A single verified user is restricted to successfully purchasing a maximum of 2 tickets per flash sale event.
  • BR-2 (Payment Timeout): Ticket reservation locking duration is set to 15 minutes post-order creation, after which unpaid orders are automatically closed and resources released.

docs.title: 6. Other Requirements
docs.text: • Compliance: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) collected by the system (such as ID numbers and phone numbers) must comply with GDPR and national data security regulations, utilizing masked storage and encrypted transmission.

docs.title: Appendix A: Glossary
docs.text: Term Acronym Definition Event-Driven Architecture EDA An architectural pattern centered around the production, detection, consumption, and reactive processing of events. Command Query Responsibility Segregation CQRS An architectural pattern separating data read operations from mutation write operations into distinct models. Software Requirements Specification SRS Software Requirements Specification document. Architecture Decision Record ADR Document capturing critical architectural decisions and rationales. Quality of Service QoS Service quality metrics and performance standards.

    subgraph Client Layer
        User[User Client]

        User -->|1. Query Ticket Read Request| Gateway[API Gateway]
        Gateway -->|2. Check Cache| Redis[Redis Cluster Cache Layer]
        Redis -- Cache Hit --> User
        Redis -. Cache Miss .-> DB_Read[(MySQL Slave Read DB)]
        DB_Read -. Asynchronous Refresh .-> Redis
    end

    subgraph CQRS Write Path & EDA [CQRS Write Path & Event-Driven Shaving]
        User -->|3. Click Flash Sale Command| DynamicToken[Token & Rate Limit Verification]
        DynamicToken -->|4. Lua Atomic Stock Deduction| Redis
        Redis -->|5. Publish Purchase Event on Success| Kafka[Kafka Message Queue Topic]
        Kafka -->|6. Asynchronous Subscription & Consumption| Worker[Worker Consumer Cluster]
        Worker -->|7. Persist Order Creation| DB_Write[(MySQL Master Write DB)]
        Worker -->|8. WebSocket Queue Completion Notice| User
    end
